Tuesday: Lavanya and Afreen played snakes and ladders. When Lavanya landed on a snake, she quickly moved her piece up anyway. Afreen cried, "That's cheating!" and walked off.
Thursday: Lavanya landed on a snake again. Her hand hovered. She looked at Afreen and slid down.
Next week: Afreen won. Lavanya sighed. "Good game. My turn to go first next time?"

qa.q: What game did Lavanya and Afreen play?
qa.a: They played snakes and ladders.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's hand hovering on Thursday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was tempted to cheat again but was thinking about fairness and Afreen's feelings.

qa.q: What helped Lavanya choose fair play?
qa.a: Seeing Afreen walk off after the cheating likely showed her that cheating ruins the game.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel when Lavanya says "Good game"?
qa.a: Afreen would probably feel happy and trust Lavanya more as a friend. 😊

grounding: It shows a child learning to accept the outcome of a game without cheating.

Dark clouds were rolling in over the park. There was only one free swing, and a long queue. Mehak and Bhupen both ran to it.
"Me first!" Bhupen said.
"No, me!"
They both held the chains. Then Mehak let go. "You first. Ten pushes, then me."
Bhupen swung, counting. At ten, a raindrop fell. He jumped off. "Your turn, quick!" Mehak got three swings before the rain came down.

qa.q: How many pushes did Mehak suggest Bhupen take?
qa.a: Mehak suggested ten pushes.

qa.q: What might Mehak have felt letting Bhupen go first?
qa.a: Mehak may have felt frustrated but also wanted to be fair so they could both have a turn.

qa.q: What went well in how they shared the swing?
qa.a: They agreed on a clear number of pushes and Bhupen jumped off when his turn ended.

qa.q: How might it feel for Mehak to get only three swings?
qa.a: Mehak may feel disappointed, but glad to still get a turn because Bhupen kept the deal.

grounding: It shows children taking turns fairly on a swing despite time pressure from the rain.

passage:
In their Chandigarh colony, Deepika and Ira were racing toy cars across the courtyard, a chalk line marking the finish. Ira's car crossed the line first, just ahead. Deepika's face went red. She crouched and looked hard at the line, then at Ira. For a moment she said nothing. "You won."
"Again?" asked Ira.
Deepika nodded. "But this time I go first."
Ira grinned. "Fine."

qa.q: Where were Deepika and Ira racing their toy cars?
qa.a: They were racing across the courtyard in their Chandigarh colony.

qa.q: What does Deepika's red face suggest she felt when Ira won?
qa.a: It suggests she was upset or disappointed about losing.

qa.q: What could a parent praise Deepika for?
qa.a: They could praise her for admitting Ira won and asking fairly for another turn.

qa.q: How might Ira feel about Deepika saying "You won"?
qa.a: Ira may feel happy and respected, and keen to play again.

grounding: It shows a child accepting the outcome of a game and taking turns fairly.

passage:
"Six! My turn again!" Ganga shouted, grabbing the dice.

"No, you had your turn," Manjula said. "It's mine."

Ganga held the dice behind her back. "But I want to win."

"If you cheat, it's not a real win."

Ganga pouted. Then she slowly handed the dice over. "Okay. Your turn."

Manjula rolled a two. Then Ganga's snake came, and down she slid. Her lip wobbled. "I lost."

"Play again?" Manjula asked.

Ganga sniffed, then nodded. "I'll be yellow this time."

qa.q: What number did Manjula roll?
qa.a: Manjula rolled a two.

qa.q: What did Ganga want when she held the dice behind her back?
qa.a: She was so eager to win that she felt tempted to take an extra turn.

qa.q: What helped Ganga give the dice back?
qa.a: Manjula calmly explained that cheating is not a real win, which helped Ganga accept it was not her turn.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel when Ganga agrees to play again?
qa.a: Manjula probably feels happy that the game can continue and that Ganga accepted the loss.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young child accepting turn-taking and a game's result without cheating.

passage:
Note from Tenzin, football coach, Saturday:

Sachin, six, wanted to take every penalty in practice today. When I said it was another child's turn, he kicked the grass and said it wasn't fair. I asked him to count how many kids were waiting. He counted and went quiet. Later his team lost the mini-match. He was upset but shook hands with the other side.

What I did next: I told him it's hard to wait and hard to lose, and he did both well today 👍

qa.q: What did Sachin want to do in practice?
qa.a: He wanted to take every penalty.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when told it was someone else's turn?
qa.a: He felt it wasn't fair and was frustrated, kicking the grass.

qa.q: What helped Sachin accept his turn?
qa.a: Tenzin asked him to count how many children were waiting, which helped him see the fairness himself.

qa.q: How might the other team see Sachin shaking hands after losing?
qa.a: They would likely see him as a good sport, even though he was upset.

grounding: A coach's note shows a young child learning to wait his turn and accept losing fairly.

passage:
On the verandah of a house in a Kerala village, Imran and Elizabeth, both five, played snakes and ladders.
Imran rolled a four. His counter landed on the big snake's head.
“No!” He looked at Elizabeth, then quickly moved his counter one square forward.
Elizabeth frowned. “That's cheating.”
Imran's ears went red. He moved it back and slid down the snake all the way to the bottom. “Okay. Your turn.”
Elizabeth rolled. Imran watched, arms crossed, but he waited.

qa.q: What did Imran roll?
qa.a: He rolled a four.

qa.q: How did Imran feel when Elizabeth said “That's cheating”?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, with red ears, but chose to play fair.

qa.q: What could an adult say to Imran after the game?
qa.a: They could tell him it was hard to slide down and that playing fair made the game fun for both.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel when Imran moves his counter back?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and happy that the game is fair again.

grounding: A five-year-old stops himself from cheating and accepts the outcome of a game.

passage:
In a small square in Lisbon, Camila and Bilal, both five, played hopscotch with chalk.
Camila hopped to square six and her foot landed right on the line.
“Line!” Bilal said.
Camila stopped. “No, it wasn't.” She looked down. It was.
She sighed loudly. “Okay. Your turn.”
Bilal hopped all the way to ten and back. Camila clapped, a bit slowly.
Then she took the stone and began again from one.

qa.q: Where did Camila's foot land?
qa.a: Her foot landed right on the line.

qa.q: How did Camila feel when she had to give up her turn?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and frustrated, sighing loudly, but accepted it.

qa.q: What could Bilal do to keep the game friendly?
qa.a: He could cheer for Camila on her next turn so she feels included.

qa.q: How might Bilal feel when Camila accepts the rule?
qa.a: He probably feels the game is fair and enjoys playing with her.

grounding: A five-year-old accepts losing her turn in hopscotch without cheating.

passage:
In the school hall, Ms Keerthana played music for musical chairs. When it stopped, Ira, five, was left standing.
Her lip wobbled. She tried to squeeze onto the edge of Kavin's chair.
“Ira,” said Ms Keerthana gently. “You're out this round.”
Ira stood still, fists tight. Then she took a big breath and walked to the side.
“Want to be my music helper?” Ms Keerthana asked.
Ira nodded and pressed the button for the next round, smiling a little.

qa.q: What did Ira try to squeeze onto?
qa.a: She tried to squeeze onto the edge of Kavin's chair.

qa.q: How did Ira feel when she was left standing?
qa.a: She felt upset and disappointed, with a wobbling lip and tight fists.

qa.q: What did Ms Keerthana do that helped Ira accept being out?
qa.a: She calmly stated the rule and then gave Ira a helper role, so she still felt part of the game.

qa.q: How might Kavin feel when Ira tries to share his chair?
qa.a: He might feel annoyed or confused, since he won his chair fairly.

grounding: A five-year-old accepts being out in musical chairs with a teacher's gentle support.

passage:
I'm Kashish, and I was watching Mahima play snakes and ladders with the older kids.
Mahima rolled a two. Her counter stopped one square below a big ladder. She stared at the dice. Her hand hovered. I thought she might push the counter up one more.
She didn't. She sighed loudly and left it there.
Next turn, the boy after her got the ladder. Mahima's lip wobbled, but she said, "Your turn was good," and waited.
She lost that game. She set up the board again anyway.

qa.q: What number did Mahima roll?
qa.a: A two.

qa.q: What does Mahima's loud sigh suggest?
qa.a: Mahima felt disappointed and tempted to cheat, but she chose to leave her counter where it landed.

qa.q: How could an adult support Mahima after a game like this?
qa.a: An adult could quietly tell Mahima they noticed she played fair even when it was hard.

qa.q: How might the older kids see Mahima after this game?
qa.a: They might trust her more as a player, since she didn't cheat and was kind about their good turns.

grounding: A classmate watches a child resist moving her counter and accept losing a game.

passage:
The first day of summer holidays, Binita pushed past everyone to the front of the swing queue.
Two days later, Farida didi brought a sand timer to the park. "When the sand runs out, it's the next person's turn." Binita watched the sand, fidgeting. When it ran out, she hopped off, frowning, and let the next girl on.
A week later, a small boy tried to jump in front of her. Binita held up her hand. "Not your turn. Wait for the sand." Then she turned it over for him when her own time was done.

qa.q: What did Farida didi bring to the park?
qa.a: A sand timer.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she hopped off frowning?
qa.a: Binita felt reluctant and a bit annoyed, but she still gave up the swing when the sand ran out.

qa.q: Why did the sand timer help Binita?
qa.a: The timer made turns clear and fair, so Binita could see when her turn would come and when to stop.

qa.q: How might the small boy see Binita turning the timer over for him?
qa.a: The small boy would probably feel it was fair and be glad that Binita made sure he got his turn.

grounding: Over the summer holidays a child learns to wait for her turn with a sand timer.

passage:
The Christmas party was in a tiny room with too many chairs and too little space. The music kept stopping as the speaker crackled.
Sabina and Ishita were the last two, circling one chair. The music stopped. Ishita sat first.
Sabina's face crumpled. For a second she grabbed the chair's back as if to pull it. Then she let go.
"You won," she mumbled, eyes wet.
Ishita offered her half the chocolate prize. Sabina took it, and asked if they could play once more.

qa.q: How many chairs were left when Sabina and Ishita were circling?
qa.a: One chair.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she grabbed the chair's back?
qa.a: Sabina felt disappointed and tempted to pull the chair, but she let go and accepted losing.

qa.q: How could a grown-up support Sabina after this game?
qa.a: A grown-up could tell her they saw how hard it was to let go and that losing fairly like that takes courage. 👍

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Sabina says "You won"?
qa.a: Ishita is likely relieved and happy, and sharing the prize shows she cares about Sabina too.

passage:
The Holi colours had dried on the courtyard wall when Nirmala, six, and her friend Lavanya started a game of hopscotch in the dust.
Lavanya threw her stone. It landed right on the line. "That's in!"
Nirmala looked at it. On the line meant out. She wanted to win badly; she'd lost twice already. Her cousin Kishan, sitting on the wall, watched them.
"It's on the line," Nirmala said. "Your turn is over."
Lavanya pouted, then nodded. Nirmala hopped all the way to the end and won.
Kishan clapped. "Fair and square." Lavanya smiled. "Next game, I'm winning."

qa.q: Where did Lavanya's stone land?
qa.a: It landed right on the line.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when she looked at the stone?
qa.a: Nirmala felt tempted and frustrated, wanting badly to win after losing twice, yet she still spoke up fairly.

qa.q: What would you advise children who disagree about a rule during a game?
qa.a: They could look at the rule together and agree on it, and have a friend like Kishan help check when it's close.

qa.q: How does Lavanya react to being told her turn is over?
qa.a: Lavanya is disappointed and pouts, but she accepts it and stays friendly, even joking about winning next time.

grounding: Shows young children accepting whose turn it is and the result of a game without cheating.
